questions.q: How close will Apophis come on 13 April 2029, and is that closer than the satellites that carry TV and weather pictures?
questions.do: Read the cards under Apophis, 13 April 2029 and look at the picture beside them.
questions.a: About 31,640 km above the surface, from JPL’s distance of 38,011 km from Earth’s centre. Geostationary satellites orbit at 35,793 km, so Apophis passes inside their ring.

questions.q: Using the energy bench, how much energy did the Chelyabinsk rock carry, and why does a rock twice as wide carry so much more?
questions.do: Click Chelyabinsk 2013 under What if it hit?, read Energy, then double the width.
questions.a: About 400 kilotons of TNT, matching the published 400–500 kt. Twice the width means 8 times the volume and mass, so 8 times the energy at the same speed.

questions.q: Why does the chart of passes look crowded in the past month and nearly empty in the months ahead?
questions.do: Look at the Passing Earth chart either side of today and read the note under it.
questions.a: Most small asteroids are discovered only days before or after they fly by. The future list holds only the ones already known, so it always looks emptier than it will turn out.

questions.q: On the Palermo scale, which known asteroids rate between −2 and 0, and what does that range mean?
questions.do: Read the top rows of The risk list and the explanation above it.
questions.a: Only 1950 DA (29075) and Bennu (101955). Between −2 and 0 means the risk merits careful monitoring; below −2 means no likely consequences.

questions.q: Where is India’s crater lake made by a meteorite, and how big is it?
questions.a: Lonar, in Buldhana district, Maharashtra: 1.8 km wide and 150 m deep, punched into Deccan basalt. It is usually dated to about 52,000 years ago.
